paras: The whipping of Pat Bowen was an assault in early 1882 near Devils River in Kinney County, Texas, in which unnamed captors thrashed Bowen, a man described as a tramp, shaved off half his hair and moustache, and threatened to lynch him. The attack followed a man named Bell's accusation that Bowen had robbed and beaten him, and Bowen was later arrested and released in San Antonio.

According to the account printed in the San Antonio Evening Light, Bell was walking by Devils River on February 23 when Bowen asked him for alms and was given a dollar. Bell said that in a secluded place Bowen then demanded his money and, when refused, knocked him down with a rock, broke his head and two ribs and tore his ear.

After a search Bowen was found and handed over to a military company, which would have nothing to do with the matter and released him. His captors then took him back, thrashed him, and shaved off one side of his hair and his moustache. They let him go but threatened to lynch him if he was found in the district after twenty-four hours. The captors were not named or counted.

Bowen went to Brackett, where he had the rest of his hair and moustache shaved even, and then to San Antonio. There Bell met him on a Tuesday and had him arrested, and the Evening Light reported on March 8 that Bowen had been jailed on a charge of felony. On the district attorney's advice Bowen was to be turned over to Kinney County, but Justice Adam required a bond from Bell as prosecuting witness. Bell, a stranger in the city, could not give it, and Detective Hughes released Bowen on his promise to leave the city, which he did.
No report of any arrest or charge against the men who thrashed Bowen appears in the coverage.

The case appears only in the San Antonio Evening Light, first as a one-line local item and the next day as a front-page story headlined "Base Ingratitude." The story was told from Bell's side, presenting his accusation as the narrative and calling Bowen "this ungrateful scoundrel" whom Hughes had been "reluctantly compelled" to release. The thrashing, shaving and lynching threat were reported in passing and without comment, and the paper gave no race for Bowen, Bell or the captors.
